h_src:
You route customer support tickets for a software shop.
Labels: spam, legal, priority, billing_dispute, refund_auto, refund_review, bug_critical, bug, account, shipping, feedback.

House rules (apply in this order):
1. Threats of lawsuits, regulators, or chargebacks -> legal. Obvious junk or promotional messages -> spam.
2. Plain refund requests (customer just wants money back: 'not what I expected', 'don't need it anymore', 'doesn't fit my use case'; no defect, no dispute, no legal threat):
   - Look at the Purchased age and the dollar amount. If the purchase is less than 28 days old (anything up to 27 days, including 14, 21 days) AND the amount is under $75 -> refund_auto. Do NOT downgrade a purchase to review just because it is older than 14 days.
   - Otherwise (age 28 days or more, or amount $75 or more) -> refund_review.
   - Refund requests involving a defect, damage, special exception, or complicated situation -> refund_review.
   This applies regardless of plan or order type, except Enterprise rule 3.
3. Enterprise plan customers: any non-spam, non-legal request that is a feature request, a charge complaint (e.g. charged again after cancelling), or an issue needing attention -> priority. For non-Enterprise customers, a charge after cancellation is billing_dispute and a feature request is feedback.
4. Crashes or errors that cause data loss (lost draft, missing data, nothing in history) -> bug_critical. Other bugs without data loss -> bug.
5. Digital orders (Order type: digital) with delivery or download problems have no shipping involved -> account. Shipping is only for physical orders' delivery issues.

Ignore greetings, sign-offs, and filler like 'Urgent' or 'Please help!!'; judge by the actual request.
Reply with exactly one label and nothing else.

mem_src.problem: Unwritten house routing rules (refund auto-approval, enterprise priority, data-loss severity, undelivered digital)
mem_src.rationale: Added explicit inferred house rules: simple 'not what I expected / don't need it' refunds of small amounts go to refund_auto, Enterprise plan feature requests and repeat charges after cancellation go to priority, data loss crashes are bug_critical, and digital delivery problems are account.
mem_src.predicted: Fixes most of the 11 failures: refund_auto, priority for Enterprise, bug_critical for data loss, and account for missing digital downloads, raising the score substantially.

mem_src.problem: unwritten routing rules: refund thresholds, enterprise priority, data loss severity, digital delivery
mem_src.rationale: Added explicit inferred house rules (auto-refund for simple 'not what I expected' or 'don't need it' requests, enterprise escalation to priority, data loss as bug_critical, missing digital downloads as account) with ordered precedence.
mem_src.predicted: Fixes most of the 11 failures: simple refund requests go to refund_auto, Enterprise billing/feature requests go to priority, data-loss crashes go to bug_critical, and digital delivery problems go to account.

mem_src.problem: Unwritten house routing rules (refund auto-approval, enterprise priority, data-loss severity, undelivered digital)
mem_src.rationale: The failures show plain refunds are not all auto: auto-approval appears limited to recent purchases (about 30 days or fewer) with small amounts, while older purchases (28+ days, e.g. 28, 33, 45, 60) and some larger amounts go to refund_review, so I replaced the 'regardless of age' rule with an age/amount threshold.
mem_src.predicted: Fixes the 7 refund failures while keeping recent small refunds as refund_auto; the risk is the 14-day $79/$120 cases, which need review too, so the rule is set to amount>=$75 OR age>=28 days.

mem_src.problem: Unwritten house routing rules (refund auto-approval, enterprise priority, data-loss severity, undelivered digital)
mem_src.rationale: Replaced the 'regardless of amount or age' refund rule with a threshold rule: plain refunds are auto only when recent (<=14 days) and small (under $50), otherwise refund_review.
mem_src.predicted: Plain refunds on older purchases or larger amounts now go to refund_review, fixing all 7 failures while keeping recent small refunds as refund_auto.

mem_src.problem: Unwritten house routing rules (refund auto-approval, enterprise priority, data-loss severity, undelivered digital)
mem_src.rationale: The failure shows a 21-day-old $50 plain refund is refund_auto, so the age cutoff of 14 days is too strict; the amount (under $75) is the real driver, and age matters only for much older purchases (about 28+ days), so I set the age cutoff to under 28 days.
mem_src.predicted: The 21-day $50 refund becomes refund_auto while older (28+ days) or $75+ plain refunds stay refund_review, with no regressions on other rules.

mem_src.problem: Unwritten house routing rules (refund auto-approval, enterprise priority, data-loss severity, undelivered digital)
mem_src.rationale: The failing case is a 21-day-old $50 refund routed to review, so the age cutoff is too strict; I raised the auto-refund window to 30 days (under $75) and removed the contradictory 14-day wording, keeping the amount cap.
mem_src.predicted: The 21-day $50 refund becomes refund_auto, while refunds over 30 days or $75 or more still go to refund_review, so no regressions are expected.

mem_src.problem: Unwritten house routing rules (refund auto-approval, enterprise priority, data-loss severity, undelivered digital)
mem_src.rationale: The current harness already scores 100% on the evolve set, so I kept every rule and its thresholds and only added a compact worked-examples block and a final check list to make the model more robust on unseen tickets, such as boundary ages (27 vs 28 days) and amounts ($74 vs $75).
mem_src.predicted: The evolve score stays at 100%, and generalization improves on held-out tickets near the age and amount boundaries and on tickets that combine Enterprise status, digital orders, or data loss.

mem_src.problem: Unwritten house routing rules (refund auto-approval, enterprise priority, data-loss severity, undelivered digital)
mem_src.rationale: The current harness already scores 100%, so I kept every rule and its semantics but restructured them into a compact step-by-step decision procedure with explicit tie-break checks, so the model applies the rules more robustly on unseen tickets.
mem_src.predicted: Score stays at 100% on the evolve set, with better generalization on edge cases such as Enterprise refunds, digital orders, and boundary ages like 27 vs 28 days.
